questions.stem: A typical human somatic cell has which chromosome complement?
questions.explanation: Diploid human somatic cells ordinarily have two sets of 23 chromosomes, for 46 total.

questions.stem: A typical human sperm or egg contains how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Gametes carry one set: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome.

questions.stem: What do homologous chromosomes normally have in common?

choices.text: The same gene loci in the corresponding order

questions.explanation: Maternal and paternal homologues carry matching loci but can carry different alleles.

questions.stem: A newly replicated chromosome consists of which structures?

choices.text: Two sister chromatids joined at a centromere
Two unrelated chromosomes joined by cytoplasm

questions.explanation: DNA replication creates sister chromatids; chromosome count does not simply double when chromatids appear.

questions.stem: Which best defines an allele?

choices.text: An alternative form of a gene

questions.explanation: Different alleles can occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

questions.stem: A gene's locus is its _____.
questions.explanation: Locus names the chromosomal position, not an allele's effect.

questions.stem: Which option is a human gamete?
questions.explanation: Eggs and sperm are reproductive cells carrying a haploid chromosome complement.

questions.stem: What separates during anaphase I of meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I reduces chromosome-set number by segregating homologues.

questions.stem: What separates during anaphase II?
questions.explanation: Meiosis II resembles mitosis in separating sister chromatids.

questions.stem: During which stage is crossing over classically initiated?
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes synapse and exchange DNA in prophase I.

questions.stem: Why does a tetrad contain four chromatids?

choices.text: It joins two already replicated homologues

questions.explanation: Each of two homologous chromosomes has two sister chromatids.

questions.stem: How many rounds of DNA replication ordinarily precede the two meiotic divisions?
questions.explanation: DNA replicates once during premeiotic interphase; two subsequent divisions follow.

questions.stem: What creates independent assortment of chromosome pairs?

choices.text: Random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I
Separation of sister chromatids at anaphase I

questions.explanation: Homologue pairs orient independently during metaphase I, generating alternative combinations.

questions.stem: Crossing over directly exchanges DNA between which chromatids?

choices.text: Chromosomes from unrelated species in separate cells

questions.explanation: Exchanges occur between nonsister chromatids in paired homologues.

questions.stem: Which lecture example illustrates asexual reproduction?
questions.explanation: Hydra can reproduce by budding, making a new individual from one parent.

questions.stem: A clone is expected to be genetically similar to its parent, but can differ because of _____.
questions.explanation: DNA changes can occur in otherwise asexual lineages.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes mitosis from meiosis?

choices.text: Mitosis requires crossing over between homologues
Mitosis is always the same as reproduction

questions.explanation: Mitosis is a nuclear division, while asexual reproduction is a broader reproductive strategy.

questions.stem: Why do siblings of the same parents usually differ genetically?

choices.text: Each parent transfers identical entire diploid genomes
All gametes contain the same chromosome combination
Alleles from one parent are erased
Gametes contain varied allele combinations, and fertilization is probabilistic

questions.explanation: Meiotic assortment, recombination and gamete union produce combinations.

questions.stem: What forms directly when two ordinary animal gametes fuse?
questions.explanation: Fertilization creates a zygote containing genetic contributions from both parents.

questions.stem: Which mechanism changes how preexisting chromosomes are combined, rather than creating new DNA alleles?

choices.text: DNA damage causing a new sequence

questions.explanation: Independent assortment recombines inherited chromosomes; mutation supplies novel DNA variants.

questions.stem: Why is fertilization important to typical sexual life cycles?

choices.text: It restores a diploid set from two haploid gametes
It halves the zygote's chromosome complement
It always produces genetically identical siblings

questions.explanation: Fusion combines the two haploid contributions into one zygote.

questions.stem: What did Mendel's pea experiments challenge?

choices.text: The existence of variation in pea traits
The idea that hereditary traits permanently blend

questions.explanation: Discrete hereditary factors can be transmitted without permanently merging.

questions.stem: A heterozygote Aa produces ordinary gametes containing what?

choices.text: An Aa chromosome pair in each gamete
Either A or a, not both in one gamete

questions.explanation: The two alleles segregate into different gametes during meiosis.

questions.stem: Which genotype is heterozygous at a single locus?
questions.explanation: A heterozygote has different alleles at the locus.

questions.stem: Which genotype is homozygous recessive?
questions.explanation: Both copies carry the same recessive allele in aa.

questions.stem: Under complete dominance, what does an Aa heterozygote express?

choices.text: A permanent averaging of two phenotypes

questions.explanation: Complete dominance describes the phenotype of the heterozygote, not removal of the recessive allele.

questions.stem: Which item is a phenotype rather than a genotype?
questions.explanation: Flower color is an observable character; allele combinations are genotypes.

questions.stem: Why were controlled crosses central to Mendel's evidence?

choices.text: They linked defined parent traits to predictable offspring ratios
They showed all offspring are exact parental clones
They proved no genes influence development

questions.explanation: Counting offspring from deliberately chosen crosses revealed discrete inheritance patterns.

questions.stem: For Aa × Aa, what genotype ratio is expected?
questions.explanation: The four equally likely gamete combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa.

questions.stem: Under complete dominance, Aa × Aa gives what expected phenotype ratio?
questions.explanation: Three of four genotypes include the dominant allele.

questions.stem: Which cross best identifies whether a dominant-phenotype individual is AA or Aa?

choices.text: Cross with another unknown dominant phenotype
Cross with a genetically unrelated species

questions.explanation: A recessive tester reveals whether the unknown individual transmits a recessive allele.

questions.stem: What offspring ratio is expected from Aa × aa under complete dominance?
questions.explanation: Half of the gametes from Aa carry a; all tester gametes carry a.

questions.stem: A 1:1 expected ratio in a cross guarantees what about a family of two offspring?

choices.text: No particular exact outcome; ratios are probabilistic

questions.explanation: Independent offspring outcomes can deviate substantially from expected frequencies in small families.

questions.stem: For two independent 1/2-probability events to both occur, multiply to get _____.
questions.explanation: The product rule gives (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4.

questions.stem: What does a Punnett square display?

choices.text: Physical chromosome positions in a nucleus
The true allele frequency of every population
Possible offspring allele combinations and expected frequencies

questions.explanation: Punnett squares model probabilities from specified parental gametes.

questions.stem: Under independent assortment and complete dominance, what is the expected AaBb × AaBb phenotype ratio?
questions.explanation: The classic two-locus cross produces four phenotype classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

questions.stem: When is Mendel's simple independent assortment assumption most likely to fail?

choices.text: When the genes are physically close on the same chromosome
When the genes are on different chromosomes
When a Punnett square is used

questions.explanation: Genes near each other on one chromosome are genetically linked and tend to cosegregate.

questions.stem: What does 'multiple alleles' mean in a diploid population?

choices.text: One ordinary person always carries five alleles at one locus
Each chromosome has more than two DNA strands
More than two versions of a gene may exist across individuals

questions.explanation: A population can have many allele types even though a typical diploid individual has at most two at one locus.

questions.stem: Which ABO genotype expresses both A and B antigen types?
questions.explanation: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant in AB individuals.

questions.stem: A variant in one gene changes several distinct body traits. This illustrates _____.
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy means one gene contributes to multiple phenotypic effects.

questions.stem: A trait strongly influenced by several genes exemplifies _____.
questions.explanation: Many genes can contribute to one phenotype, so a simple dominant/recessive model may fail.

questions.stem: Why can genetically similar individuals display different phenotypes?

choices.text: All DNA must have mutated independently
Alleles disappear in one of the individuals
Phenotypes never depend on external conditions
Environment and development can modify expression of inherited variants

questions.explanation: Gene action occurs in environments, so phenotype is not determined by genotype alone.

questions.stem: Why does close inbreeding raise the probability of some recessive disorders?

choices.text: Mutations become immediately more frequent in every gene
The chromosome number doubles in all offspring
Relatives are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive allele

questions.explanation: Related individuals share alleles through ancestry, increasing risk of matching recessive variants.

questions.stem: Which parental situation makes a recessive single-gene disorder more likely in an offspring?

choices.text: A completely unrelated trait is dominant
Both parents carry a pathogenic allele at the same locus
One parent is unaffected and has no gene copies

questions.explanation: A recessive disease often requires inheriting pathogenic variants from both parents.

questions.stem: How can a single-gene dominant disorder differ from a typical recessive one?

choices.text: One pathogenic copy may be enough to affect phenotype
It always requires two mutated copies

questions.explanation: Dominant inheritance can produce a phenotype in heterozygotes.

questions.stem: What was the important genetic change in the Raphanobrassica example?

choices.text: Ordinary mitotic segregation alone restored the original species
Chromosome doubling after a sterile radish–cabbage hybrid formed

questions.explanation: Doubling provided chromosome partners for more regular meiotic pairing and fertility.

questions.stem: Why can allopolyploidy sometimes cause rapid plant speciation?

choices.text: A hybrid gains chromosome sets and can become reproductively isolated from parent species

questions.explanation: Combining and doubling divergent chromosome sets may create a newly fertile but isolated lineage.

questions.stem: Which change is directly associated with inbreeding?

choices.text: Transformation of autosomes into sex chromosomes

questions.explanation: Inbreeding increases the chance that both gene copies descend from a shared ancestor.

questions.stem: Why might an undoubled interspecies hybrid fail to form functional gametes?

choices.text: Its chromosomes may lack sufficiently matching partners for regular meiosis
Its DNA cannot replicate in any cell
It cannot perform mitosis under any condition

questions.explanation: Failure of chromosome pairing or segregation can produce hybrid sterility.

questions.stem: Which observation links Mendel's laws to a physical cellular mechanism?

choices.text: Chromosomes remaining stationary in every cell division

questions.explanation: Chromosome movement explains how alleles segregate and sometimes assort independently.

questions.stem: Which experimental organism did Thomas Hunt Morgan use?
questions.explanation: Morgan's Drosophila studies provided compelling gene–chromosome evidence.

questions.stem: Which property made Drosophila practical for genetic experiments?
questions.explanation: Fast breeding and four chromosome pairs simplify genetic crosses.

questions.stem: In Morgan's terminology, wild type describes _____.

choices.text: The common reference phenotype in the studied population
A guaranteed ancestral allele at every locus
An organism without any DNA variants
Any hybrid produced in a laboratory

questions.explanation: Wild type is the usual reference condition, not absence of genetic variation.

questions.stem: A white-eyed fly differing from the typical red-eyed phenotype is an example of _____.
questions.explanation: Mutant refers to a contrasting heritable phenotype in this experiment.

questions.stem: Why did sex-associated white-eye inheritance matter in Morgan's work?

choices.text: It showed genes contain no DNA
It connected a particular hereditary trait to the X chromosome
It proved all genes are on the Y chromosome

questions.explanation: Different inheritance by sex supported localization of the eye-color gene to X.

questions.stem: In the chromosome theory, Mendelian factors occupy specific _____.
questions.explanation: The theory locates genes at physical positions on chromosomes.

questions.stem: Where is a sex-linked gene located?
questions.explanation: Sex linkage refers to the gene's location on the X or Y chromosome.

questions.stem: Why can a recessive X-linked allele be expressed in an ordinary XY individual?

choices.text: The Y chromosome always carries a dominant matching allele
The allele must first become mitochondrial
There is often no second X copy at that locus to mask it

questions.explanation: An XY individual is usually hemizygous for most X-linked loci.

questions.stem: A Y-linked DNA marker generally follows which inheritance path?

choices.text: To every descendant regardless of sex chromosomes
From a Y-bearing father to Y-bearing offspring
From mothers to all children equally

questions.explanation: The Y passes chiefly along paternal Y-lineages.

questions.stem: Which structure contains its own genetic material outside the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have genomes separate from nuclear chromosomes.

questions.stem: In humans, mitochondrial DNA usually comes from _____.

choices.text: A new bacterial infection at every birth

questions.explanation: Most human mitochondrial DNA is maternally transmitted with the egg cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Which statement best characterizes genetic chimerism?

choices.text: One allele disappears from every nucleus
All identical twins are automatically chimeras
All human red blood cells contain chloroplasts
Cell populations from distinct zygotic lineages occur in one individual

questions.explanation: Chimerism refers to genetically distinct cell lineages from different zygotic origins, not simply heterozygosity.

questions.stem: Why is 'all organelle DNA is always maternally inherited' too absolute?

choices.text: Organelles are always inherited only from sperm in humans
All plant cells have exactly two chromosome sets
Some plant organelles can be transmitted paternally or biparentally

questions.explanation: Uniparental organelle inheritance is common, but patterns vary across taxa.

questions.stem: Which isotope did Hershey and Chase use to track bacteriophage DNA?

choices.text: Radioactive oxygen as the protein-specific label

questions.explanation: DNA contains a phosphate backbone, so ³²P labels its phosphorus.

questions.stem: Which isotope primarily labeled the phage protein coats?
questions.explanation: Proteins can contain sulfur-bearing amino acids while DNA lacks sulfur in its normal backbone and bases.

questions.stem: After infection, blending and centrifugation, where was most DNA-associated ³²P found?
questions.explanation: The labeled phage DNA was associated with bacterial cells, which formed the pellet.

questions.stem: What did the ³⁵S-rich supernatant mainly indicate?

choices.text: DNA was absent from infecting phages
Many phage protein coats stayed outside bacterial cells

questions.explanation: Protein coats were largely left outside, and blending removed them from bacterial surfaces.

questions.stem: What central conclusion did the Hershey–Chase experiment support?

choices.text: DNA carries genetic information injected by the tested bacteriophages
Proteins are not made in organisms

questions.explanation: The DNA label tracked into infected bacteria and their progeny more strongly than protein-coat label.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of blending infected bacteria in the experiment?

choices.text: Detach outer phage coats from bacterial surfaces

questions.explanation: Blending helps separate remaining viral protein from bacteria before fractionation.

questions.stem: What type of biological agent is a bacteriophage?
questions.explanation: Hershey and Chase used phages to follow material transferred during bacterial infection.

questions.stem: Which two DNA bases are purines?
questions.explanation: A and G have the two-ring purine structure.

questions.stem: Which group includes the pyrimidines of DNA?
questions.explanation: C and T are single-ring bases in DNA; RNA usually uses U rather than T.

questions.stem: In ordinary double-stranded DNA, which pairing is correct?

choices.text: A with T and G with C
A with G and T with C
A with C and G with T
A with A and C with C

questions.explanation: One purine pairs with one pyrimidine, keeping helix width approximately constant.

questions.stem: Which combination describes RNA compared with DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains ribose and usually U where DNA contains T.

questions.stem: What provides the covalent framework of each DNA strand?
questions.explanation: Nucleotides are joined along each strand by phosphodiester bonds.

questions.stem: Why does complementary pairing make DNA copying possible?

choices.text: Each old strand can guide assembly of a matching new strand
The DNA sequence is destroyed before copying

questions.explanation: Template-guided base selection reproduces sequence information.

questions.stem: Why should the lecture's 'one error per 10 billion bases' be treated cautiously?

choices.text: Error rates depend on the organism and repair conditions
Every cell has exactly the same absolute rate
Every mutation is repaired after reproduction
DNA polymerase never makes a mistake

questions.explanation: Very low final error rates reflect proofreading and repair and vary by system.

questions.stem: Transcription directly synthesizes which molecule from a DNA template?
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA based on a DNA template.

questions.stem: What is translation?

choices.text: Ribosomes read mRNA to assemble a polypeptide

questions.explanation: Translation converts mRNA codon information into amino-acid sequence.

questions.stem: What role does mRNA play in ordinary gene expression?

choices.text: It is the enzyme that carries out meiosis
It carries a coded sequence from DNA to the ribosome
It serves as the chromosome spindle
It is always the same as a DNA double helix

questions.explanation: Messenger RNA is the template read by translating ribosomes.

questions.stem: What length is a codon?
questions.explanation: The genetic code uses triplets of RNA bases.

questions.stem: Where does translation take place?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes coordinate tRNA and mRNA during amino-acid chain assembly.

questions.stem: Which is the immediate molecular product of translation?

choices.text: A newly synthesized DNA double helix

questions.explanation: The amino-acid chain can fold or be modified into a functional protein.

questions.stem: What does the near universality of the genetic code help explain?

choices.text: Every codon codes for a distinct amino acid
Many genes can be expressed after transfer between species
DNA cannot be transferred across lineages
Each species has its own completely unrelated codon meanings

questions.explanation: Shared coding conventions allow many foreign protein-coding genes to be read by another organism's translation machinery.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'descent with modification'?

choices.text: Inherited features change across generations in branching lineages
Every organism evolves during a single afternoon
Traits never vary between parents and descendants
Life progresses through one fixed ladder toward humans

questions.explanation: Evolution involves ancestry plus heritable change through time.

questions.stem: Why is an evolutionary tree drawn as branches rather than a ladder?

choices.text: Modern organisms all evolved one after another in a single chain
One living species must be the ancestor of every other living species
Evolution has a single predetermined endpoint
Lineages split, diversify and share ancestors

questions.explanation: Branching ancestry captures divergence and common descent.

questions.stem: Who established binomial nomenclature through Systema Naturae?
questions.explanation: Linnaeus helped standardize two-part scientific names in the eighteenth century.

questions.stem: Which historical view is especially associated with Lamarck?

choices.text: Acquired characteristics being inherited through use or disuse
Natural selection based on inherited population variation

questions.explanation: Lamarck's proposed mechanism is not the accepted general account of adaptive evolution.

questions.stem: Which major scientific book appeared in 1859?

choices.text: Systema Naturae in its first edition

questions.explanation: Darwin's book presented an extensive case for descent with modification and natural selection.

questions.stem: Who independently formulated the idea of natural selection alongside Darwin?
questions.explanation: Wallace's parallel insight led to joint presentation of their ideas in 1858.

questions.stem: Who was called 'Darwin's Bulldog' for defending evolutionary thinking?
questions.explanation: Huxley was a prominent advocate of Darwinian evolution.

questions.stem: What three features allow natural selection to change a population?

choices.text: Equal fitness for all variants without any environmental difference
Heritable variation, differential reproductive success, and repeated generations
Every organism changing DNA on demand

questions.explanation: Selection favors inherited variants whose carriers contribute more descendants in the relevant environment.

questions.stem: Which change is best attributed to genetic drift?

choices.text: An allele becomes rare by chance after a small population bottleneck
Camouflage variants consistently survive better against predators
A new DNA base substitution creates an allele

questions.explanation: Drift is random sampling of alleles, not directed survival advantage.

questions.stem: A barrier divides one population into geographically isolated groups. This event is _____.
questions.explanation: Vicariance is geographic subdivision; subsequent drift or selection may cause genetic divergence.

questions.stem: Which example most directly demonstrates sexual selection?

choices.text: A chromosome acquires a second chromatid
Peahens prefer males with particular courtship displays
DNA is replicated during S phase

questions.explanation: Mating preferences can favor traits that change reproductive success.

questions.stem: In evolutionary biology, an individual's fitness is most directly related to _____.

choices.text: Its position on a fixed tree of life
Its contribution of descendants to later generations

questions.explanation: Evolutionary fitness measures reproductive contribution in context, not strength or longevity alone.

questions.stem: Evolution by a population-genetic definition can involve a shift in _____.

choices.text: The number of bones in one individual during adulthood
The number of pages in a textbook

questions.explanation: Inherited allele proportions can change via mutation, selection, drift and migration.

questions.stem: Which process produces an allele sequence that did not previously exist?

choices.text: An existing allele being counted twice

questions.explanation: Mutation introduces new sequence variants; other processes change their distribution.

questions.stem: Which event is a prezygotic reproductive barrier?

choices.text: A hybrid embryo dies after fertilization
A fertile zygote later becomes infertile
Two populations mate during different seasons
A hybrid develops but is sterile

questions.explanation: Timing differences can prevent mating or fertilization before a zygote forms.

questions.stem: Which is a postzygotic barrier?

choices.text: A hybrid is sterile after developing
Potential mates occupy different habitats and never meet

questions.explanation: Sterility of a formed hybrid reduces gene flow after fertilization.

questions.stem: Why is reproductive isolation important in speciation?

choices.text: It limits gene exchange, allowing lineages to diverge
It forces all populations to retain identical allele frequencies
It guarantees every hybrid is fertile
It prevents mutation in both populations

questions.explanation: Reduced gene flow can permit genetic differences to accumulate independently.

questions.stem: What is a limitation of the biological species concept?

choices.text: It requires no information about reproduction
It forbids all hybridization between named species
It is difficult to apply to fossils and many asexual organisms

questions.explanation: Species boundaries are complex; interbreeding criteria are not universally usable.

questions.stem: What is speciation?

choices.text: DNA copying in S phase only
Elimination of all alleles from a population
Evolutionary formation of distinct species lineages

questions.explanation: Long-term divergence and isolation can produce separate lineages.

questions.stem: Which pattern fits a mass extinction?

choices.text: Many diverse lineages disappear over a geologically short interval
One allele increases through selection in a single local population

questions.explanation: Mass extinctions remove many species across broad taxonomic and geographic scales.

questions.stem: What does adaptive radiation describe?

choices.text: Diversification into numerous lineages exploiting different ecological opportunities
Rapid loss of every population in a clade
Only the pairing of sister chromatids
A single gene acquiring a new allele

questions.explanation: Adaptive radiations can follow ecological opportunities or extinctions that open niches.
